book.title: Cervical Artery Dysfunction and Upper Cervical Instability
book.lead: A safety chapter. Learn to recognise rare but dangerous conditions before treating the neck.

blocks.text: The internal carotid and vertebral arteries carry blood to the brain through the neck. A dissection is a tear in the inner wall of an artery that can lead to a clot and a stroke. Dissection can happen spontaneously or after minor trauma, and the early symptom can be neck pain or headache that looks like a musculoskeletal problem. This is why physiotherapists must screen before treating the neck [Ref – to verify: IFOMPT cervical framework].

Upper cervical instability means excessive movement between the skull, C1 and C2, usually from ligament damage (trauma) or weakness (rheumatoid arthritis, Down syndrome, connective tissue disorders). Unstable joints may compress the spinal cord or arteries.

blocks.label: TEACHER'S VOICE
body: No screening test is reliable enough to "clear" a patient for safe neck treatment. Your protection is a careful history, recognising the patterns, and choosing low-risk treatment when in doubt.

rows: Upper neck and back of the head, often one-sided, unusual and severe

blocks.text: The "5 Ds and 3 Ns" (classic posterior circulation symptoms)

items: **D**izziness, **D**iplopia (double vision), **D**ysarthria (slurred speech), **D**ysphagia (difficulty swallowing), **D**rop attacks. **N**ausea, **N**ystagmus (jerky eye movements), **N**umbness (often of the face).
Add: ataxia (unsteady walking).

blocks.text: E1. Positional vascular tests (for example sustained rotation)

Positional tests were traditionally used to screen for arterial insufficiency. Current frameworks state that their diagnostic accuracy is uncertain and a negative result does not exclude arterial disease [Ref – to verify]. If used, they must be stopped immediately at the first symptom.

blocks.text: Defer all cervical manipulation and end-range mobilisation until vascular and instability concerns are fully resolved by a doctor.

steps: **Before any neck treatment, ask:** new or unusual pain? neurological symptoms? recent trauma? vascular risk factors? instability risk?
**Any yes with neurological signs:** emergency referral.
**Risk factors but no signs:** choose low-force treatment (exercise, mid-range mobilisation); avoid manipulation; monitor; explain.
**No concerns:** proceed with the appropriate neck pathway, using informed consent.

items: Physiotherapy does not treat dissection or instability directly. The physiotherapist's role is recognition, referral and later rehabilitation after medical management.
After medical clearance, rehabilitation is gentle, active, and avoids end-range or high-velocity techniques in the cervical spine.
Patients with rheumatoid arthritis or Down syndrome should not receive upper cervical manipulation without specialist clearance.

blocks.text: At each visit, re-ask about neurological symptoms. A new symptom at any point overrides the plan.

items: **Can a negative positional test clear a patient for manipulation?** No. Accuracy is uncertain; history and clinical reasoning matter most.
**List the 5 Ds.** Dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, drop attacks.

**A 40-year-old has new severe right neck pain after a fall while playing cricket, and now a drooping right** **eyelid. What do you suspect?** Possible carotid dissection with Horner syndrome. Emergency.
**Why is rheumatoid arthritis important for neck treatment?** It can weaken upper cervical ligaments, causing instability.
**What is your safest default when you are unsure?** Avoid high-velocity or end-range techniques, use exercise and gentle methods, and seek medical advice.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Recognise vascular and instability warning signs.
Perform a cranial nerve and coordination screen.
Explain why screening tests cannot "clear" a patient.
Choose the correct urgent action.
